title: How To Improve Student Politeness
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that direct lessons on politeness fail with today's students because rudeness is culturally coded as cool, making explicit instruction backfire into frustration. Instead, he claims politeness spreads through a subconscious mechanism: modeling it yourself, consistently and unapologetically, without ever explicitly teaching a lesson on it. His concrete technique focuses on three specific courtesy behaviors -- please and thank you, hello and goodbye, excuse me and after you -- modeled by the teacher and lightly reinforced with prompting questions like 'What do you say?' He adds two important constraints: never hold students accountable (i.e., never punish) for forgetting a courtesy, since it isn't a rule violation, and never praise or reward politeness either, because the goal is for students to internalize it as inherently valuable rather than performing it for external approval.
points: Direct politeness lessons backfire because students associate rudeness with being culturally cool, so the shift must happen subconsciously through modeling.
Focus modeling on three specific behaviors: please/thank you, hello/goodbye, and excuse me/after you.
Never hold students accountable for forgetting a courtesy -- it isn't a rule violation and shouldn't be treated as one.
Never praise or reward polite behavior either, since the goal is for politeness to be internalized as inherently valuable, not performed for reward.
quotes: The more polite students are, the fewer class rules are broken. Therefore, if we improve politeness, then we can save a lot of time and trouble holding students accountable.
The reason is because for students being polite feels lame and old-fashioned. Sad but true. The culture they're used to is generally rude and dismissive, which they associate with being cool.
It’s a method that works on a subconscious level to cause students to become more polite without you ever mentioning it.

It’s important to mention that you shouldn’t hold students accountable if they don’t say please, goodbye, or excuse me, for example. Forgetting common courtesies doesn’t constitute breaking SCM class rules.
For it to become part of the culture of your classroom, as well as who your students are as people, it must be something they recognize as having value in and of itself.
